description: FOUR friends from Karachi giving NASA's abandoned Moon and Mars machines a voice through an interactive web story. Skills: web dev, AI, content creation, marketing. Team full, excited to meet you!
summary:
The Unfinished Mission is an interactive, cinematic, scroll-driven web experience that retells the stories of
NASA hardware left behind on other worlds for school age explorers (age 8 to 14). Instead of presenting
these machines as space junk, it treats them as robotic pioneers and shows how they worked and what they
taught us.
Challenge addressed: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the
Moon and Mars.
Format chosen: an interactive web-based experience (HTML, CSS, JavaScript with 3D graphics), one of the
formats the challenge quite explicitly.
Core message: every machine we left behind was a promise that we'll keep exploring and exploring.
details:
The Unfinished Mission

1. What does the project. How does it work?

The Unfinished Mission is a cinematic scroll‑driven educational web experience made for young explorers aged 8–14. The Unfinished Mission turns NASA’s space hardware stories into immersive journeys showing how machines left behind on the Moon and Mars helped scientists learn and push exploration forward.

The Unfinished Mission guides visitors through three destinations:

  • The Moon – Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle: The Unfinished Mission shows how the lunar rover let astronauts travel across the Moon beat mobility limits and gather geological samples.
  • Mars – Opportunity Rover: The Unfinished Mission tells the story of a rover that was built to work for 90 sols but kept going for 15 years studying Martian rocks and giving evidence that water once flowed on Mars.
  • Deep Space – Voyager 1: The Unfinished Mission introduces visitors to Voyager 1 a robotic explorer that is still traveling outside our solar system. The Unfinished Mission explains how Voyager 1 kept working and how it deals with the challenge of sending messages over distances.

Each destination follows six storytelling stages: Enigma, Machine, Traverse, Simulation, Science and Legacy. The Unfinished Mission gives visitors 3D scenes, engineering explanations, discovery cards and interactive activities.

The Unfinished Mission also offers three hands‑on learning experiences:

  1. Lunar Rover Simulator: The Unfinished Mission lets visitors drive a lunar rover while watching its distance, direction and range from the lander showing the 5 km walk‑back safety limit.
  2. Mars Evidence Lab: The Unfinished Mission introduces visitors to minerals such as hematite, jarosite, gypsum and clays and explains how these clues help scientists study ancient water on Mars.
  3. Interstellar Ping: The Unfinished Mission shows radio communication delays between Earth and Voyager 1 helping visitors see why signals take a day to travel one way.

A child‑astronaut companion called EVA‑01 guides visitors through the Unfinished Mission with short age‑appropriate explanations.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The Unfinished Mission makes space science and engineering easier for audiences. Of asking students to read complex documents the Unfinished Mission shows mission histories through pictures interactive exploration and simple simulations.

The Unfinished Mission’s main benefits include:

  • Engagement: The Unfinished Mission makes NASA mission histories more interesting and easier to understand for school‑age learners.
  • STEM learning: The Unfinished Mission introduces ideas about robotics, engineering, planetary science, navigation, geology and communication technology.
  • Learning through interaction: The Unfinished Mission lets visitors test simplified mission scenarios of only reading facts.
  • Scientific understanding: The Unfinished Mission links engineering choices with the discoveries each spacecraft or vehicle made.
  • Accessibility: The Unfinished Mission supports layouts, keyboard navigation skip links, reduced‑motion preferences and mobile‑friendly navigation.
  • Critical thinking: The Unfinished Mission encourages visitors to ask questions about how machines work and how scientists explore far worlds.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The Unfinished Mission’s intended impact is to change how young audiences see space hardware that has finished its mission or is far from Earth.

Space exploration is often shown through astronauts, new launches and active missions. The Unfinished Mission says that the machines that helped make these achievements possible also have stories that deserve to be told. Their engineering, challenges and science deserve recognition.

The Unfinished Mission wants to make these stories easy to read for a generation and to spark curiosity about science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM).

The Unfinished Mission hopes students will see that a machine does not need to return to Earth to be useful. The Apollo 15 rover broadened exploration of the Moon Opportunity changed our view of ancient Martian places and Voyager 1 still pushes humanity’s reach into interstellar space.

Ultimately the Unfinished Mission wants to inspire learners to care more about scientific discovery, technological progress and the future of space exploration.


4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?


The Unfinished Mission was built with web technologies and open‑source libraries.

Programming languages:
  • JavaScript (ES Modules and JSX)
  • HTML
  • Css



Frameworks and development tools:
  • React 19 for the user interface and component architecture.
  • Vite for development and production builds.
  • Three.js, for 3D graphics.
  • React Three Fiber and Drei are tools that let us put 3D scenes inside a React app.
  • GSAP 3 and ScrollTrigger provide animations that follow the scroll and feel cinematic.
  • Lenis makes scrolling smooth but it is turned off on touch devices.
  • Web Audio API creates background sound that is generated by code.
Design and visual technologies:
  • Modular vanilla CSS and design tokens keep styles organized.
  • Newsreader, Space Grotesk and Fredoka are the fonts we use.
  • WebGL draws the 3D scenes on the screen.
Development, version control and deployment:
  • Google Antigravity helps us write code with AI support.
  • Claude from Anthropic guides planning prompt writing, story drafts, documentation and research.
  • GitHub keeps all code versions. Lets the team work together.
  • Vercel hosts the site and manages deployments.

No special hardware or external APIs were needed. The whole experience runs in a web browser. Works on both desktop and mobile devices.

The 3D spacecraft, rover and environmental scenes were built with code using shapes and textures instead of official NASA 3D models.

5. How is your project creative?

Our creative approach treats space hardware as pioneers that have their own journeys, challenges and legacies rather than showing them as abandoned objects.

We blend storytelling with interactive science learning. Of showing long paragraphs of history the experience slowly reveals the story as visitors scroll through different settings.

Several creative elements set this project apart:

  • A cinematic opening sequence gives a start to the mission.
  • EVA-01, a child astronaut companion guides visitors from one destination to another.
  • Three‑dimensional lunar, Martian and deep‑space environments give a feeling of exploration.
  • Scroll‑driven animations reveal information bit by bit linking visual events to science explanations.
  • Interactive simulations let visitors try simplified engineering and communication challenges.
  • Each chapter follows a steady storytelling structure that links the machine’s purpose, journey, science contribution and legacy.

The mix of real mission histories, interactive simulations and cinematic presentation makes an experience that brings science topics closer to younger audiences.

6. What factors did your team consider during development?

Our team thought about key factors while designing and building the project.

  1. Accuracy: Mission information was researched using NASA and NASA/JPL resources, including the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) Apollo mission records, Mars Exploration Rover resources and Voyager mission information. Claims that need verification were marked for review instead of being shown as facts.
  2. Target audience: The experience was made for children aged eight to fourteen. We used language that's easy to understand short explanations, visual discovery and interactive learning.
  3. Accessibility and usability: We added layouts, keyboard support skip links, reduced‑motion options, mobile navigation and screen‑reader support for typed text. We also considered WebGL fallback functionality.
  4. Performance: Three‑dimensional graphics and animations can be heavy on devices. We used lazy‑loaded scenes, lighter 3D rendering on mobile and a WebGL error fallback to make the experience smoother, on devices.
  5. User experience: We thought about navigation, storytelling flow, clear typography, sound controls and the option to skip the opening.
  6. Use of AI and resources: AI tools helped with planning, coding, writing and development but the team directed the work reviewed the results and decided on the final experience. NASA imagery and third‑party assets were checked for proper attribution and use.

Through these thoughts our team aimed to build an experience that balances creativity, education, technical work, accessibility and responsible science communication.

Our Message: Every machine we left behind was a promise that humanity would keep exploring.
